title: Intersectional Barriers: Examining the Combined Experience
before: Explore how two or more conditions can combine into a single barrier, and how to respond to the whole connected route.

turns.text: Intersectional Barriers: Examining the Combined Experience is about barriers that come from more than one condition at once. It’s for staff examining complex service or workforce conditions, and for supervisors and managers considering how connected requirements affect opportunity. The course asks you to follow the whole route a person has to travel, rather than reviewing each piece separately.

The opening case shows why: a notice offers a daytime phone explanation and asks people to confirm online. Someone can’t use the confirmation page and can’t attend the phone explanation. Each part might look usable on a list of available methods, yet the person still can’t complete the task. The barrier lives in how the parts connect.

The course grounds this in Crenshaw’s foundational analysis, which examined how separate race and sex categories can obscure Black women’s experiences. The lesson it carries forward is analytical: look at how conditions interact. Race, disability, gender, and other dimensions matter, but they don’t let us predict a particular person’s circumstances from identity.

It also keeps racialized experience in view by asking whose concerns receive credibility, which expectations are treated as normal, and whether comparable requests get comparable responses. The course says not to dissolve racism into a general access list, and it’s just as clear that identity alone doesn’t establish what happened in a particular decision. Both cautions hold together.

One tool I find useful is mapping rules, resources, and interpretation in sequence. What must the person do, what helps make it possible, and how is their response understood? A request for another route can turn into a negative label, and that label can influence the next decision. Following the sequence shows where the conditions build on each other.

The course introduces disability justice as a movement framework connecting intersecting experience, whole-person value, and collective access. It’s careful to say this isn’t adopted DHS policy or a formula for individual needs. It also points out that separate reports about two groups don’t establish the experience of people who belong to both.

You’ll practice in three situations: a service application doesn’t work with a person’s reading tool, and the phone alternative isn’t explained in a language they can use. A team repairs a development assessment while practice assignments still depend on private nominations. And a participant describes repeating their concern between two contacts, each addressing only one part.

Those examples share a theme, which is that a nominal alternative isn’t always equivalent. A recording may provide information but miss the discussion where later assignments are offered. When you compare responses, the course asks you to look at the baseline, a single-condition repair, and a connected response, using the same purpose and leaving unknown costs unknown.

Near the end, you’ll rewrite an explanation that simply says several identities caused a person’s difficulty. The supported version describes how specific conditions interacted and left no usable way to complete the task. You’ll also consider what social context and missing comparison you’d keep before interpreting a wider pattern, which is the bounded conclusion the course builds toward.

The reflection asks you to recall a situation where two requirements worked poorly together, and what examining each one separately would have missed. You can keep it private, and no one needs to disclose personal history. The aim is to identify one interaction and one question that could change your explanation.

As you start, think about a process in your own work that involves more than one step or team, perhaps a notice and a follow-up, or an assessment and an assignment. Where could two usable parts fail together? Bring that example along, and see how the combined view changes what you would recommend.

guidance.title: Follow the sequence
guidance.text: Mapping rules, resources, and interpretation in order shows how one condition sets up the next. A person asks for another route because a page doesn’t work for them. If that request is then recorded as reluctance, the label can follow them into a later decision. Each step may seem reasonable on its own, but the barrier becomes visible when you read them together.

guidance.title: Where the parts meet
guidance.text: Think of one process you know where people move between steps or teams. Where does one part hand the person to the next, and who checks whether they can actually complete the whole task? What would you need to learn from the people who use that route before deciding which connection to examine first?
